FP86 is titled **“Green Cities Facility”**. It is implemented through the **European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD)** as the **accredited entity**, and (in this B.37 document) lists the host countries as **Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Moldova, and Tajikistan**. The **GCF financing** is printed as **EUR 87 million**, with **total financing** printed as **EUR 100 million**. The proposal is associated with **Board meeting B.37 (2023)**. [189_12-status-approved-fps-adding-host-countries-respect-fp086-gcf-b37-07, cover pages]

Additional details surfaced in the retrieved pages:
- The document notes an ability to **request additional commitment from GCF up to a total amount of EUR 100 million**, with any such request to be made **up to one year before the programme closing date**. [189_12-status-approved-fps-adding-host-countries-respect-fp086-gcf-b37-07, p. 2]
- The programme is described as addressing climate challenges through **four components**: (i) policy and strategic support; (ii) technical assistance and capacity development (including infrastructure investments); (iii) capacity-building of key stakeholders; and (iv) facilitating access to green finance/capital markets. Its investment focus is stated as **six sectors: agriculture, energy, forestry, water resources, urban transport, and municipal energy systems** (e.g., district heating, waste-to-energy). [189_12-status-approved-fps-adding-host-countries-respect-fp086-gcf-b37-07, p. 2]
- The “updated supporting documents for restructuring paper” list includes items such as **NDA no-objection letters, feasibility study, integrated financial model (with sensitivity analysis), term sheet/cost breakdown, ESIA/ESMP (if applicable), appraisal/due diligence reports (if applicable), maps, and implementation timetable**. [189_12-status-approved-fps-adding-host-countries-respect-fp086-gcf-b37-07, p. 39]

Retrieval did not surface (in these excerpts) the full original FP86 proposal narrative (e.g., detailed budget by component, full results framework targets, or detailed implementation arrangements beyond the prompts shown), so I can’t provide those specifics from this evidence.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V10.0 | PAGE 48

## Barriers for Service Providers

### Climate-smart rice farming is at its nascent stage in Thailand: aspects of the emission and/or mitigation potential of climate-smart farming have been posted or synthesised, rolled-out by foundation projects, but baseline projects, but they have not been promoted and disseminated at a large scale nor in an integrated manner. The lack of awareness among farmers about the benefits of climate-smart technology and equipment carries substantial risk due to the unclear business case (particularly for smallholder farmers) compared with the well-established and well-understood sugar cane service provider sector. There is also a perception that the climate-smart rice service provision model is not financially viable, compared with the well-established and well-understood sugar cane service provider sector.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V10.0 | PAGE 61

## Output 2: Enhancing farmers' access to finance for climate-smart farming services and technologies.

### Outcome 2.1: Service providers invest in and offer climate-smart technologies to rice farmers.
- Activity 2.1.1: Strengthening market linkages and standards for sustainable rice and biomass sector
- Activity 2.1.2: Strengthening the enabling national and policy environment for climate-smart rice farming.

### Outcome 3: Government policies and funds are geared towards climate-smart rice.
- Output 3.1: Strengthened institutional and market environment for climate-smart agriculture
- Activity 3.1.1: Strengthening market linkages and standards for sustainable rice and biomass sector
- Activity 3.1.2: Thaï Rice Facility and ThaiGAP implementation
- Activity 3.1.4: Regional exchange and peer-to-peer learning

## Figure 12: Project Design

1. Rice is Thailand’s most important food crop, accounting for roughly half of the country’s agricultural land and employing 18 million smallholder farmers. However, rice farming is also a significant contributor to the country's greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, mainly through methane from paddy fields.
2. Smallholder rice farmers in Thailand are vulnerable to climate change due to changing rainfall patterns, as well as increasing frequency and severity of flooding and droughts.
3. The project will focus on promoting adaptation and mitigation results from the rice farming sector in Thailand. If approved, it will be the first GEF project to focus solely on transforming the rice sector into a more sustainable one by providing smallholder farmers with access to a suite of climate-smart technologies and practices, as well as farmer-friendly financial services.

Rice farmers' adoption of, and investment in, climate-smart technologies and practices (Outcome 1);

(b) Service providers' supply of, and investment in, climate-smart technologies (Outcome 2); and

(c) Strengthening of the institutional and business environment for climate-smart rice farming.

From this perspective, the project's outcomes and outputs focus on the fundamental components that will enable the transformation towards a more sustainable and resilient productivity of Thailand’s rice farming (through climate-smart practices and technologies) and its adaptive capacity (through institutional strengthening, improved market conditions and mastery of climate change knowledge). The adoption of these technologies and practices will also enable a low-GHG emission system.

B.5 Justification for GCF funding request

B.5.1 Additionality

281 The Thai Rice Project addresses mitigation and adaptation priorities identified by the government of Thailand in its NDC and the SAP. It targets a key economic sector – rice farming – that is emissions-intensive and especially vulnerable to climate change. The Thai Rice Project builds on a strong baseline of existing policies, programs, and practices for sustainable agriculture and climate-smart rice farming from a diverse set of public and private sector actors in order to address an identified set of barriers. The project will generate significant co-benefits through the mobilization of substantial additional funding from the private sector, involving actors along the entire value chain.

climate-resilient rice insurance and the Thai Agricultural Standard (TAS) for sustainable rice, the Thai Rice Project addresses all three pathways.

114. The project logic can be stated as follows:

IF farmers and service providers are capacitated, equipped and able to apply climate-smart technologies and practices, and their linkages to markets are strengthened, and if public policies and incentives are in place to support these changes, then the following will happen:
THEN paradigm shift will be achieved through the development of a climate-smart rice sector built upon self-outsourcing business models, mainstreamed climate-smart technologies, market-based value chains, and improved livelihoods.

BECAUSE rice farming in Thailand will be timely set upon a climate-resilient and low-emission pathway, with significant investment for its implementation.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUNDING PROPOSAL (V.10.3) PAGE 141

## Sustainability

The sustainability of the current rice farming model is questionable. Since 2015 global climate change has revealed the vulnerability of the rice sector to extreme weather events, and GHG emissions continue to increase and reach record levels despite significant problem despite repeated government efforts to reduce them in the rice sector.

### Low

#### Paradigm shift would see the development of a self-sustaining climate-smart rice sector in which farmers are able to adopt climate-smart technologies and practices with little or no external interest to do so and because they have access to information, awareness, financial and market-based incentives needed to overcome initial adoption barriers.

The Thai Rice Project is assessed as having high sustainability potential. The project will:

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V.10.0 | PAGE 108

## Activity 3.1.2 Strengthening the enabling environment for climate-smart rice farming

### A capacity development strategy for TAS verified rice (equivalent) is developed.

#### Government bodies shift policy and institutional programmes (sub-national agricultural policies, Strategic Plan for the Agriculture Sector, etc.) into a climate-smart framework (e.g., Climate Change Committees), onto a climate change project implementation plan.

- The T-VER Rice Scheme is coupled to the voluntary carbon market coupled to the TAS.
- The Thai Rice Facility is established as an implementation coordination body and commercial operations entity. It will develop a strategy for the rice sector, etc.), to be integrated into the climate-smart rice and other related climate-smart rice projects are supported with grants.

#### All activities are implemented in collaboration with the World Rice Conference side-event and knowledge sharing events.

## The Thai Rice Project Will

The Thai Rice Project will enable climate-smart rice farmers—increasingly, women farmers—to adapt to a changing climate (Outcome 1) while simultaneously reducing GHG emissions (Outcome 2).

### Project Design and Outcomes

#### Bottom-up Approach
- **Behavioral Changes**: Triggered at the level of the farmer through behavioral changes.
- **Adoption of Climate-smart Practices**: Climate-smart practices (Output 1.1) and climate-smart technologies will be made available by service providers—industrialized, mechanized, and well-equipped service providers supported by a strong institutional framework.

#### Financial Support
- The climate-smart rice that is produced will be verified and sold at higher market prices.
- A financial support mechanism will be established to ensure the sustainability of this sector, designed and implemented to unlock additional revenue flows to support Thailand’s transition towards a low-carbon economy (Outcome 3).

## Development of green employment in the region

The programme is strengthening regional integration among Amazon countries, having common issues, by supporting the regionalization of bioeconomy value chains and integration initiatives. This holistic and systemic approach aims to promote sustainable development in the Amazon Region, promoting inclusion and sustainable business models.

### The proposed programme considers a set of interlinked individual projects, unified under a single funding proposal

The programme is designed to enhance the resilience of target value chains and ecosystems in the Amazon region by enabling the conditions for their long-term sustainability. Interlinked individual projects contribute to common objectives and strategies that are aligned with the priorities of the Green Climate Fund (GCF) mitigation and adaptation result areas of efficiency and effectiveness at an scale.

# Bioeconomy: Private role in bio-businesses and forest conservation

25. Because of the Amazon’s diverse biological, land and water resources, the bioeconomy[1] follows the ideal framework for the development of sustainable, productive models and practices in AFOLU in the Amazon region. The bioeconomy is defined as a set of economic activities that are based on the use of the Amazon's natural capital and forests (from this point forward defined as bio-businesses, see [5]). This concept includes the production of goods and services from forest resources while conserving them and reducing GHG emissions. In parallel, being conscious of risks and vulnerabilities in the mainstreaming of adaptation and mitigation strategies is essential to ensure that the region’s response to future climate-related impacts already unavoidable to this day (Table 4).

Furthermore, as per the Second NDC of Nepal, currently around 5% of households use electric induction stoves and this is expected to increase to 30% by 2030. The project contributes significantly to the achieve the target on the use of electric stoves. Strengthened supply chain, expansion of the manufacturing base in the country, will project, will proliferate across the country without external interventions even after the project period.

# Fiduciary

The AEPC will act as both the AE and the EE and will have a separate PIU to execute the project.

### Project specific execution

Medium

### GCF portfolio concentration

Low

### Compliance

High

## Results monitoring and reporting

This project is a mitigation activity aimed at the dissemination of CCS in Nepal. Through the establishment of various facilities and incentive mechanisms, the project aims at inducing behavioral change among households to shift from using non-renewable biomass and fossil fuel-based cooking solutions to clean cooking options.

answer: La proposition de financement du GCF qui soutient la riziculture intelligente face au climat en Thaïlande est **« Strengthening Climate-Smart Rice Farming – Thai Rice GCF »**, soumise par **Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit GmbH (GIZ)**. Cette identification apparaît dans la **lettre de non-objection** de l’Autorité nationale désignée (NDA) de la Thaïlande, qui fait explicitement référence à ce projet et à la proposition correspondante [61_gcf-b37-02-add05-funding-proposal-package-fp214, p. 202].

Cette identification apparaît dans la **lettre de non-objection** de l’Autorité nationale désignée (NDA) de la Thaïlande, qui fait explicitement référence à ce projet et à la proposition correspondante [61_gcf-b37-02-add05-funding-proposal-package-fp214, p. 202].

Development Strategy (S.T.)

Economic development relies on climate-resilient technologies in rice cultivation as a priority need.

The Adaptation Needs Assessment (ANA) for Thailand lists 5 technology priorities, including weather forecasting and early warning systems, crop technology improvement (drought tolerance), water optimization and disease and pest control. These are identified as pressing needs, precision agriculture measures (including water management and post-harvest management) and post-harvest technology.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V10.0 | PAGE 48

## Barriers for Service Providers

### Climate-smart rice farming is at its nascent stage in Thailand: aspects of the emission and/or mitigation potential of climate-smart farming have been posted or synthesised, rolled-out by foundation projects, but baseline projects, but they have not been promoted and disseminated at a large scale nor in an integrated manner. The lack of awareness among farmers about the benefits of climate-smart technology and equipment carries substantial risk due to the unclear business case (particularly for smallholder farmers) compared with the well-established and well-understood sugar cane service provider sector. - **FP214 (Thai Rice)** : financement GCF demandé = **EUR 38.17 million** (p.114, C.1(a) / règle C.1(a)) [61_gcf-b37-02-add05-funding-proposal-package-fp214].

  - **49,751,264** *(devise non imprimée)* (p.8, A.10 Grant) [02_gcf-b42-02-add16-funding-proposal-package-fp274]
  - **USD 40,751,254** (p.40, C.1(a) / règle C.1(a)) [02_gcf-b42-02-add16-funding-proposal-package-fp274]

Dear Mr. Glémarec,

1. We refer to the programme entitled “The Amazon Bioeconomy Fund” as included in the funding proposal submitted by IDB to us on May 5th, 2021.
2. The undersigned is the duly authorized representative of the Secretariat for International Economic Affairs, Ministry of Economy, the National Designated Authority for Brazil.
3. Pursuant to GCF decision D.068, the content which we have acknowledged to have reviewed, we hereby communicate our no-objection to the programme as included in the funding proposal.

   a) The government of Brazil has no objection to the programme as included in the funding proposal.

# GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V2.1 | PAGE 28 OF 82

B

## 2.2 Equitable access to finance for bio-businesses in the Amazon

Equitable access to finance is a key element of the GCF’s strategy to increase global investment flows to early-stage bio-businesses in the Amazon region in the form of direct equity, equity-like instruments and other financial products. The GCF will provide funding through its own funds under administration by the IDB (such as IDB Lab) and other co-finance. These schemes are considered effective tools to maximize the potential impact of financing operations in early-stage high-potential bio-businesses. They can be used for both equity investments and equity-like investments while offering more value for innovative companies. Equity will be used for more mature bio-businesses (i.e., those that have already demonstrated a proof-of-concept or are at an earlier viable product phase), have positive revenues, and are looking for gaining market traction.

### GREEN CLIMATE FUND FUNDING PROPOSAL V2.1 PAGE 26 OF 82

#### B

49 With a view to using a multi-stakeholder approach (including investors, banks, project developers, producers, specialized advisory institutions, and RAD institutions) the Programme focuses on enabling the conditions to increase the flow of funds to bio-businesses in the bioscience of the Amazon. The Programme will be implemented through three components: (i) Sovereign investment loans; (ii) Sovereign investment grants; and (iii) Concessional financing solutions for bio-businesses.

50 In order to achieve Programme goals and in line with the theory of change, a multi-component structure is proposed. Since not all components and activities might be relevant or applicable in all participating countries, the Programme will include an indicative framework that aims to provide a list of possible –not mandatory– uses for the funds at the country level.

### Program Components

### GCF Financial Support

GCF provides three types of financial support: IUSD 137.5 million grant contribution including reimbursable grant, which is 49 per cent of total cost; IUSD 208.6 million loan (IUSD 6.5 million interest); and IUSD 279 million (47 per cent) from GCF. The accredited implementing entity (AIE) for the funding proposal is the World Bank Group. The total cost of the funding proposal is IUSD 597 million including IUSD 279 million [47 per cent] from GCF. The accredited implementing entity (AIE) for the funding proposal is the World Bank Group.

## ARCAFIM Contractual Arrangements

ARCAFIM has two level of contractual arrangements - upstream and downstream. In the upstream arrangement, the IFAD intends to receive financial resources from the international financiers (including the GCF with IFAD) and channel such GCF Proceeds to Host Bank in accordance with the terms and conditions agreed between IFAD and the Subsidiary Loan Agreement.
